It finds that the angels’ repeated emergence from desolation embodies beauty’s unsettling persistence, suggesting that art illuminates an uncertain future even amid darkness and exhaustion.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Not, Angels, They

outputs.L1:
Not that I understand things. Angels don’t walk toward the ship in the old engraving, where the moon throws a river of light—the way angels would walk the ocean, if they wanted to walk. They don’t. They hover, with a lot of space between them and what shines like waves. Which can’t be a choice, for the angels or the engraver, who was, in fact, Gustave Doré, after sleeping off the ancient mariner Coleridge left behind under guilt and regret and an albatross’s weight.

Which isn’t much, but they are big animals, four feet across, counting the wind involved and rain. Doré waking to a room not really of wings. I guess a stirring, something in the black expanse he hoped to razor into the copper plate—no, a graver, not a razor at all.

Beauty does terrify: a bare nothing but stop. As in angels. Abrupt. Still, to cut them, their flight, into metal takes a while. His hands stiff, Doré under a deadline, no doubt, like the small, endlessly later rest of us: we do what we do and do until it’s not what we do.

Nevertheless, angels. Why did they keep coming, one by one, radiant dark of a mind paused before this most desolate given: water at night. That it floods a future not even in the picture.
outputs.L2:
I don’t claim to know. In the old illustration, the angels do not advance toward the vessel. The moon lays a luminous road across the sea—the route they might take if angels traveled on foot. But they do not step; they float, suspended well above what resembles glittering surf. That distance could hardly have been intentional, either for the angels or for the artist, Gustave Doré, emerging from sleep into the world of Coleridge’s Ancient Mariner: guilt, remorse, and the burden of an albatross. The bird’s weight is slight, though its body is large, spanning four feet when wind and rain are included.

Doré wakes in a room that does not literally contain wings. Perhaps there is only a faint disturbance in the darkness, something he means to score into copper with a sharp edge—except the instrument is a graver, not a blade. Beauty can be frightening: an empty command to halt, sudden and absolute, like the angels themselves. Yet fixing their airborne stillness onto metal requires time. His fingers grow rigid. Surely Doré works against a deadline, as all of us, arriving much later, continue our tasks over and over until they cease to be ours.

And still the angels appear. Why do they continue coming, singly, each a shining darkness born from a mind arrested by the bleakest fact imaginable: the ocean after nightfall? Its waters spill forward into a future that lies beyond the image.
outputs.L3:
Gustave Doré’s engraving presents angels hovering above a moonlit ocean rather than walking across the water toward the ship. Suspended between darkness and light, the figures appear as sudden, supernatural presences over the vast and desolate sea. Their position in the sky intensifies the distance between the human world below and the spiritual realm they seem to inhabit.

The poem connects Doré’s artistic vision to Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner*. Like Coleridge’s poem, Doré’s image evokes guilt, regret, and the heavy burden symbolized by the albatross. The ocean becomes more than a setting: it is a space of isolation and judgment in which past actions cannot easily be escaped. Against this background, the angels may suggest mercy or redemption, but their beauty also remains unsettling and remote.

Doré’s painstaking method of engraving gives physical form to an imagined darkness and the stirring of wings. Through prolonged, difficult labor, fleeting visions are transformed into figures cut into copper. This contrast is central to the poem’s portrayal of artistic creation. Beauty appears terrifying, abrupt, and almost instantaneous to the viewer, yet the image that produces this effect depends on patience, precision, and sustained effort.

The recurring angels illuminate the emptiness of the nighttime water without completely dispelling its darkness. They reveal the sea’s desolation while also pointing beyond it, toward a future that lies outside the visible boundaries of the picture. In this way, the engraving holds terror and hope together: the present remains haunted by guilt and loneliness, but the angels suggest that the story may continue beyond what the image allows us to see.
outputs.L4:
The poem begins as a meditation on Gustave Doré’s engraving of angels hovering above a moonlit sea, but it gradually becomes an inquiry into the nature of artistic creation itself. Doré’s image offers a scene poised between revelation and catastrophe: the sea appears vast and desolate, the night is heavy with uncertainty, and yet the angels rise above the water in an otherworldly light. They do not simply resolve the darkness below them. Instead, their radiance makes that darkness more visible, creating an atmosphere in which beauty and terror remain inseparable.

The poem’s fragmented imagery and abrupt self-corrections reproduce the difficulty of looking closely at such a scene. Its speaker repeatedly proposes an interpretation, revises it, and begins again, as though no single description could fully contain the engraving’s emotional force. This instability also suggests the labor of creation. Like the artist trying to draw light out of darkness, the speaker struggles to make language emerge from confusion, fatigue, and doubt. The poem therefore presents art not as an effortless act of inspiration but as a process shaped by uncertainty, repetition, and the fear of failure.

Allusions to Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” deepen the engraving’s moral and psychological dimensions. The moonlit sea recalls the Mariner’s haunted voyage, while the angelic figures evoke the spirits and supernatural presences that surround his guilt. In Coleridge’s poem, the ocean is both punishment and possible redemption: it isolates the Mariner, confronts him with the consequences of his actions, and eventually becomes the setting in which his perception begins to change. Doré’s angels similarly hover between judgment and mercy. Their appearance does not erase suffering, but it hints that desolation may still contain the possibility of transformation.

At the same time, the poem connects the Mariner’s burden of guilt with the artist’s responsibility to keep witnessing and making. Creation becomes a form of return, even a kind of compulsion. Just as the Mariner must tell his story repeatedly, the artist must continue to recreate the vision, bringing the angels back out of the darkness each time. Their repeated emergence is consoling because it demonstrates beauty’s persistence, yet it is also unsettling. If beauty must continually be summoned, then it is never secure; it exists only through renewed attention and effort.

The angels therefore do not offer a simple promise of salvation. They illuminate rather than explain. Their light opens a path into the future, but that future remains obscure, suspended beyond the visible horizon. By the end, the poem locates hopeгирло not in certainty or escape, but in the act of making itself. Even amid guilt, terror, exhaustion, and darkness, art can cause the luminous forms to appear again. Beauty persists not because suffering has been overcome, but because the imagination continues to work within it.
outputs.L5:
**Not Angels**

They came at dusk, wearing kindness like borrowed coats.  
Not angels, though everyone wanted them to be.

Angels would have promised salvation. They offered something smaller: a warm meal, a steady hand, a place to sleep without fear. Their wings were only shadows cast by tired shoulders, and their halos were streetlights trembling in the rain.

They made mistakes. They lost patience. They sometimes arrived too late.

But still, they came.

And perhaps that mattered more—not angels, not perfect, not sent from heaven. Only people choosing, again and again, to care.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented free-verse prose poem inspired by Gustave Doré’s engraving for Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” focusing on angels hovering above a moonlit ocean.
counterfactuals.output:
**Above the Drowned Mast**

Moon—  
a white wound nailed to the weather.

Below, the ocean lifts its black pages,  
turning them without hands.

And there: angels—if angels are made  
of vapor, of torn linen, of grief refusing to sink—  
hover above the mast.

They do not descend.

Their faces are small lamps. Their wings  
remember storms. One bends close  
to the water’s iron ear, whispering—

nothing the living can hear.

The ship drifts on, emptied of footsteps.  
Ropes stiffen into veins. The sails hang  
like the shrouds of enormous birds.

No wind.

Only moonlight pouring its cold milk  
over plank, wave, bone.

The angels gather, pale as breath  
on a mirror. They carry no harps.  
They carry the silence after judgment.

Far beneath them, the drowned dream upward.

Far above, heaven keeps  
its terrible distance.

And the sea—  
the sea opens and closes, opens and closes,

a dark mouth  
learning prayer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental ekphrastic poem about angels, artistic labor, guilt, and water at night. Use abrupt syntax, compressed spacing, and self-corrections.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Unfinished Annunciation**

Night varnishes the museum glass.  
Behind it: an angel  
half-gesso,half-weather—

wings scraped to underdrawing,  
gold leaf worrying the dark.

The painter’s thumbprint  
still in the halo.  
Not halo—  
a debt made circular.

I stand where Mary should be,  
holding the blue  
that cost three months’ bread.

Outside,riverwater drags  
its black silk past the quay.  
Each lamp breaks there  
and keeps breaking.

The angel lifts one hand.  
Blessing—or stop.  
No,not stop.  
The gesture of someone  
who has worked too late  
and cannot feel the brush.

Feathers everywhere,carefully.  
Carelessly.  
Each white stroke another lie  
about purity.

I helped, I think.  
I mixed the lead.  
I washed the bowls  
until the sink became moonlit,  
until the moon became a stain  
we agreed not to name.

What is guilt but pigment  
refusing to dry?

At midnight the painted water  
leaks from its panel.  
A thin line first—  
then cold around my shoes.

The angel looks down  
without eyes finished.

I say forgive me.

I mean: finish me.

No—  
I mean the river  
has entered the room  
and all our golden labor  
is floating,

face-up,face-down,

toward the open door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine Gustave Doré waking after dreaming of Coleridge’s ancient mariner and beginning to engrave a dark, radiant seascape. Write a lyrical meditation that connects his graver, stiff hands, and deadline to modern creative work.
counterfactuals.output:
Gustave Doré wakes before the room has recovered its shapes. The window is a square of diluted ash; the furniture waits in darkness, half drowned. For a moment he still hears the old sailor speaking—not in words, but in the creak of rope, the wingbeat of the albatross, the bright, impossible crackle of ice.

He lights a lamp.

On the table, the copper plate holds its mute sea. His hands are stiff with sleep and labor. He opens and closes them, slowly, like shutters warped by salt. Then he takes up the graver: a small, severe instrument, more thorn than pen. It will not forgive vagueness. Every pressure must become a fact.

The deadline waits nearby.

It has arrived in the night without removing its coat. It sits among the letters from the publisher, the proofs, the promised dates. It does not care that Doré has crossed black waters in his dream, or stood beneath a moon that turned each wave into a blade. It wants the image delivered. It wants wonder by Thursday.

So he bends to the plate.

A line becomes a mast. Another becomes rigging, rain, the gaunt cheek of the mariner. Darkness is not laid down but opened: furrow by furrow, the metal taught to receive ink. Light, too, must be cut out of resistance. Radiance is made by wounding the surface with precision.

How modern this feels.

We wake now to other lamps: the blue-white screens already murmuring, already crowded with messages. Our tools are smoother. They leave no filings on the table, no crescent cuts in the thumb. Yet the hand still stiffens. The back still aches. The deadline still sits in the corner, wearing whatever century requires—commission, launch, post, pitch, revision—asking the dream to become a file before noon.

We drag a cursor across a blankness as Doré drew the graver through copper. We enlarge, undo, save. We stack translucent layers where he crossed lines. We summon oceans from code, faces from pixels, music from waveforms. The machine offers speed, but speed does not abolish the ancient difficulty: something seen inwardly must survive its passage into form.

That passage is always narrower than the dream.

The dream contains the entire storm at once—the terror, the glitter, the guilt, the bird falling through the air. The work proceeds mark by mark. The imagination is oceanic; the hand is mortal. Between them lies craft: patient, repetitive, sometimes joyless, often miraculous.

Doré pauses. Dawn begins to silver the actual roofs beyond his window. On the plate, a phantom moon burns above the ship. His fingers hurt. The publisher will complain. Some lines are wrong and cannot be wholly recalled. Still, the sea has appeared.

This may be what we ask of ourselves at every desk: not to preserve the dream intact, which is impossible, but to make a vessel for its weather. To cut carefully enough that darkness can hold light. To work while tired, while hurried, while the world demands an answer. To accept that inspiration arrives vast and untamed, and must be met by the small faithful motion of the hand.

The deadline leans closer.

Doré lowers his head and engraves another wave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem that begins “Not that I understand things” and reflects on why angels in an old engraving hover rather than walk toward a ship. Mention the albatross, copper plates, beauty, and an unseen future.
counterfactuals.output: Not that I understand things, but in the old engraving the angels hover rather than walk toward the ship because the earth has already refused them, or because mercy cannot afford to leave footprints. Beneath their weightless attention, the vessel leans into black water, its sails pale as hospital curtains. An albatross keeps one difficult sentence open above the mast. Whoever cut this weather into copper plates knew that beauty is partly pressure: the hand’s insistence, the metal’s wound, the ink settling into every deliberate scar. The angels do not board. They do not warn the sailors. Perhaps they are only the shape longing takes when history looks back at an unseen future and wants, too late, to touch it without changing its course.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an associative, stream-of-consciousness poem responding to an illustration from “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner.” Blend visual description with uncertainty, factual asides about engraving, and philosophical thoughts about terror, repetition, and desolation.
counterfactuals.output:
The mast leans—or is it the horizon  
that has forgotten how to stand?  
A moon, coin-thin, keeps no promise.  
Below it the ship is stitched into the sea  
with black hatchings, cross-hatchings,  
thousands of cuts pretending to be night.

An engraving begins in injury:  
the image entered by incision,  
or, in the nineteenth-century illustrated book,  
often translated by skilled hands into end-grain wood,  
white lines lifted from darkness.  
What looks like shadow is labor repeated—  
stroke after stroke after stroke—  
as waves are repeated,  
as guilt repeats one bird in every bird.

There: perhaps the Mariner,  
though the face is scarcely a face,  
only a pale interruption in the ink.  
His eyes may be open.  
They may be two errors left uncorrected.  
Around him the sailors lie arranged  
like dropped punctuation,  
and the ropes, stiff with silence,  
lead nowhere I can name.

Terror is not the storm.  
The storm at least is going somewhere.

Terror is the water that does not move,  
the bell that must have rung but cannot be heard,  
the same thought returning in another coat:  
I did this.  
I did this.  
Did I do this?

Even the albatross is absent  
and therefore everywhere—  
a white vacancy on the chest,  
a hinge between fact and omen.  
Birds do not mean forgiveness.  
Birds mean birds, until the mind,  
starving for a cause, makes scripture of a wing.

Look how the engraved sky crowds downward.  
Look how each line resembles its neighbor  
but never touches it.  
Is that not desolation:  
not emptiness, exactly,  
but innumerable marks  
unable to become company?

The sea keeps copying itself  
without producing a second sea.  
The dead keep dying in the eye.  
The old man keeps beginning his story  
because an ending, once spoken,  
becomes another listener.

And outside the frame—if there is an outside—  
the wedding music goes on,  
bright as metal, absurd as bread,  
while here the moon files its small cold tooth  
against the rigging,

and the ship, or the world,  
or merely this wounded block of wood,  
drifts nowhere  
with terrible precision.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
